1:1: The editor of the book is speaking as if the word of the Lord were a burden that Malachi was carrying. This is likely a reference to the serious nature of what the Lord told Malachi to say.
The editor is using the word word by association to mean what the Lord said by using words.
The author is using one part of Malachi, his hand, to mean all of him in the act of bringing the Lord’s message to the Israelites.
These notes follow the interpretation that the word Malachi is the name of a man. See the further discussion in the introduction to Malachi.
1:2: Malachi is probably not quoting an actual response from the Judeans. Rather, he is anticipating an objection, stating it, and then answering it. See the further discussion in the introduction to Malachi.
The Lord is using the question form for emphasis.
The Lord is using the names Esau and Jacob by association to mean their descendants.
1:3: The word translated as hated does not always indicate a strong antipathy or loathing.
A jackal is a wild dog that lives in the desert.
1:4: The word Edom is another name for “Esau.” the Lord uses the word Edom by association to mean Esau’s descendants.
1:5: The Lord is using one part of the Judeans, their eyes, to represent all of them in the act of seeing. The emphasis is on their eyewitness experience.
1:6: וְאִם־אָב אָנִי אַיֵּה כְבוֹדִי וְאִם־אֲדוֹנִים אָנִי אַיֵּה מוֹרָאִי
The Lord is using the question form for emphasis.
The Lord is using the word name by association to mean his reputation and authority.
1:7: The Lord is speaking as if the altar on which the priests offered sacrifices to him were a table at which he ate food.
1:8: The Lord is using the question form for emphasis.
The Lord is using the question form for emphasis.
The terms accept you and lift up your face mean similar things. The Lord is using the two terms together for emphasis.
1:9: The Lord is using one part of himself, his face, to mean all of him in the act of looking with favor on someone who was praying to him.

Malachi is probably using the term God here to contrast with the mention of “the governor” in the previous verse. The implication is that if people would not offer inferior gifts to a human being, they should certainly not offer them to God.
Malachi is using one part of the priests’ bodies, the hand, to mean all of themselves in the act of offering sacrifices.
The Lord is using the question form for emphasis.
1:10: מִי גַם־בָּכֶם וְיִסְגֹּר דְּלָתַיִם וְלֹא־תָאִירוּ מִזְבְּחִי חִנָּם
The Lord is using the question form for emphasis.
The Lord assumes that his listeners will know that by the doors he means the doors of the temple.
The Lord is using one part of the priests’ bodies, the hand, to mean all of themselves in the act of offering sacrifices.
1:11: The Lord is using the rising and setting of the sun by association to mean the east and the west.
The Lord is speaking of two extremes in order to include them and everything in between.
The Lord is using the word name by association to mean his reputation.
The Lord is using one part of himself, his name, to mean all of him.
1:12: In the same phrase in 1:7, the name “The Lord” is used. Here a title, the Lord, is used instead. It may be that in the earlier instance the Lord is speaking of himself in the third person, while in this instance the Lord is quoting what the priests would say. (In order not to misuse his name, Jews would use this title instead.) Some versions of the Bible use their representation of the divine name here, since that is what the priests meant. Other versions use the title Lord to reflect this Jewish practice and the original text of the book.
The Lord is speaking as if the altar were a tree that produced fruit.
The Lord assumes that his listeners will know that by its food he means the food allowance the priests receive from the altar.
1:13: The priests are speaking as if they wanted their listeners to Behold or look at something. They are using this term to focus their listeners’ attention on what they are about to say.
In this culture, to puff at something, blowing a small breath at it, was a symbolic action that showed contempt.
The Lord is using the question form for emphasis.
1:14: The Lord is describing one event before describing another event that would precede it.
The Lord assumes that his listeners will know that by a male, he means a healthy, unblemished male animal.
The Lord is using one part of himself, his name, to mean all of him in the act of being feared.
2:2: In contexts such as this, the word translated as listen has the specific sense of complying with what someone has said.
לֹא תָשִׂימוּ עַל־לֵב … אֵינְכֶם שָׂמִים עַל־לֵב
This is an expression that people of this culture would commonly use to mean to take something seriously or to pay attention to it.
The Lord is using one part of himself, his name, to mean all of him.
The Lord is speaking as if a curse were an object that he could send.
2:3: Behold me is an expression that people of this culture would commonly use to mean that they were about to do something.
The author is speaking of seed as if it were a living thing that he could rebuke.
The Lord is speaking as if he would spread dung on the priests’ faces. This is a vivid way of saying that he will humiliate them.
The Lord is using the word dung by association to mean the entrails of the animals that were sacrificed during festivals.
2:4: The Lord is speaking as if his commandment were an object that he could have sent.
The Lord means implicitly that he has given this commandment so that his covenant with Levi will continue.
The Lord is using the name Levi by association to mean the priests who descended from that man and who served in the tabernacle and temple in subsequent generations.
2:5: These two phrases mean basically the same thing.
The Lord is using one part of himself, his name, to mean all of himself.
2:6: The Lord is using the word mouth by association to mean what the priests said.
The people of this culture commonly said that something was … found to mean that it existed.
The Lord is using the word lips by association to mean what the priests said.
The Lord is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a path that he would walk along.
The Lord is speaking as if iniquity were a place from which people could be turned away.
2:7: The Lord is using one part of a priest, his lips, to mean all of him in the act of speaking.
The Lord is speaking as if knowledge were something that one could guard or protect.
The Lord is using the word mouth by association to mean what the priest says.
2:8: The Lord is speaking as if the priests had caused people to stumble or trip and fall. This image represents leading people to sin.

The Lord is speaking as if his covenant with the priests descended from Levi were something that they had corrupted, that is, physically spoiled and made useless, like the crops eaten by pests described with the same term in 3:11.
2:9: The Lord assumes that the priests will know that in this instance, the expression the instruction implicitly means the law of Moses and how the priests have been applying it in individual cases.
2:10: הֲלוֹא אָב אֶחָד לְכֻלָּנוּ הֲלוֹא אֵל אֶחָד בְּרָאָנוּ
Malachi is using the question form for emphasis.
הֲלוֹא אָב אֶחָד לְכֻלָּנוּ הֲלוֹא אֵל אֶחָד בְּרָאָנוּ
These two phrases mean basically the same thing.
מַדּוּעַ נִבְגַּד אִישׁ בְּאָחִיו לְחַלֵּל בְּרִית אֲבֹתֵינוּ
Malachi is using the question form for emphasis.
This is an expression that people of this culture would commonly use to mean that people were acting against others of their own community.
Malachi is speaking of the ancestors of the Israelites as if they were the fathers of the current generation.
2:11: בָּגְדָה יְהוּדָה וְתוֹעֵבָה נֶעֶשְׂתָה בְיִשְׂרָאֵל וּבִירוּשָׁלִָם
These two phrases mean basically the same thing.

Malachi is speaking as if foreign gods had daughters that the people of Judah could marry. This could mean: (1) that the Judeans have allied themselves closely with foreign gods as their worshipers, as if they had made a marriage alliance the way kingdoms did; (2) that Judean men have married foreign women, and this has led them to worship foreign gods.
2:12: Malachi is describing the people of Israel by association with their ancestor Jacob, who was also known as Israel.
Malachi is using the word tents by association to mean the community of Israel.

Malachi is speaking of two extremes in order to include them and everything in between. He is alluding to a watchman guarding a city at night (the one being awake) and someone approaching the city who is responding to the challenge, “Who is there?” (the one answering).
2:13: Malachi is making an overstatement for emphasis.
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. Malachi uses them together to emphasize how the Lord is rejecting the offerings.
Malachi is using one part of the people, their hand, to mean all of them in the act of offering sacrifices.
2:14: יְהוָה הֵעִיד בֵּינְךָ וּבֵין ׀ אֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶיךָ

In this culture, when people made promises to one another, they often did this with witnesses watching. The role of those witnesses included holding the people to their promises. The Judean men had made covenant promises to their wives when they married them. Malachi assumes that those men will know that when he refers to the Lord as a witness, he means that the Lord is holding them to those promises. The Lord is doing that by showing his disfavor through not accepting their offerings.
2:15: Malachi is using the question form for emphasis. See the introduction to this chapter for a discussion of this sentence.

Malachi is not asking the question And why one? to get information. Rather, he is asking and then answering his own question. This was a common practice of Jewish public speakers in this time period (and also in New Testament times).
Malachi is speaking as if a person’s spirit were a physical place where they could be guarded.
2:16: For a discussion of the phrase covers his garment with violence and suggestions for how to translate it, see the introduction to this chapter.
2:17: The Lord is using the term words by association to mean what the people are saying.
Malachi is using the word eyes by association to mean sight. Sight, by association, represents judgment and perspective.
The people are using the question form for emphasis.
3:1: Behold me is an expression that people of this culture would commonly use to mean that they were about to do something.
The Lord is using the word face to mean his presence by association with the way people can see the face of someone who is present.
The Lord is speaking of his coming as if it were a journey for which a way needed to be prepared.
The Lord uses this word to get the people’s attention.
3:2: וּמִי מְכַלְכֵּל אֶת־יוֹם בּוֹאוֹ וּמִי הָעֹמֵד בְּהֵרָאוֹתוֹ
The Lord is using the question form for emphasis.
וּמִי מְכַלְכֵּל אֶת־יוֹם בּוֹאוֹ וּמִי הָעֹמֵד בְּהֵרָאוֹתוֹ
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.

The Lord is using the image of standing to speak of a person being declared innocent. The idea is that if he were declared guilty, that would be like a weight too heavy for the person to carry, and the person would sink down under it.

The point of this comparison is that just as fire refines metal and soap cleans clothes, so the messenger will purify the people, that is, he will help them forsake the sins they have been committing.
3:3: The Lord is speaking as if the messenger were going to be a metalworker who was refining and purifying precious metals.
The Lord is speaking as if these priests were the sons of their ancestor Levi.
The point of this comparison is that just as gold and silver are refined to remove impurities, so the messenger will purify the people.
3:4: These two phrases mean basically the same thing.
3:5: The Lord is using the idea of being a witness to represent the entire process of judging and punishing.
The Lord is speaking of wage as if it were a person who could be oppressed.
The Lord is speaking of denying justice to foreigners as if people who did that were turning them aside from a road they were walking on and needed to stay on.
3:6: The Lord assumes that the Judeans will understand that when he says that he does not change, he means that he always keeps his promises. He promised Abraham that he would bless his descendants, and so he is still taking care of them, even though they have been disobedient.
The Lord is speaking of the Israelites as if they were the sons of their ancestor Jacob.
3:7: The Lord is speaking of the ancestors of the Israelites as if they were the literal fathers of the current generation.
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The Lord uses them together to emphasize how the people have disobeyed him.
The Lord is speaking of disobeying his statutes as if that were turning aside from a path on which one needed to walk.
3:8: הֲיִקְבַּע אָדָם אֱלֹהִים כִּי אַתֶּם קֹבְעִים אֹתִי
The Lord is not asking the question Will a human rob God? to get information. Rather, he is asking and then answering his own question.
3:9: For emphasis, the Lord is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.
3:10: The Lord is speaking of the temple as if it were his house.
The Lord is speaking of giving blessings as if he were opening windows in the sky and pouring them out.
The Lord assumes that the people will understand that by a blessing he means abundant crops.
3:11: The Lord is speaking of pests as if they were a person he could rebuke.
The Lord is speaking of crops as if they were the fruit of the ground.
The Lord is speaking of vines as if they were women who could be barren or unable to have children.
3:13: The Lord is using the term words by association to mean what the people have been saying.
3:14: The Lord is speaking of how the people have lived as if they had walked on a path.
The people are using the word face to mean presence by association with the way people can see the face of someone who is present.
3:16: This is an expression that people of this culture would commonly use to describe people speaking with one another.
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The author uses them together to emphasize how closely the Lord listened.
The author is using the word face to mean presence by association with the way people can see the face of someone who is present.
These two phrases mean basically the same thing.
The author is using the word name to represent the Lord’s reputation.
3:17: The Lord speaks as if he is preparing a day.
The point of this comparison is that just as a father tenderly cares for his son who serves him, so the Lord will tenderly care for those who serve him.
3:18: This is an expression that people of this culture would commonly use to mean to seeing something again.
The Lord assumes that the people will understand that by see, he means acknowledge.
These two phrases mean basically the same thing.
4:1: The Lord is speaking as if he wanted his listeners to behold or look at something. He is using this term to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say.
בֹּעֵר כַּתַּנּוּר וְהָיוּ כָל־זֵדִים וְכָל־עֹשֵׂה רִשְׁעָה קַשׁ
The Lord is speaking of the day of judgment as if it were an oven that would be burning people.
The Lord is speaking of wicked people as if they were stubble that his judgment would kindle and burn up.
The Lord is speaking of two extremes in order to include them and everything in between.
4:2: וְזָרְחָה לָכֶם יִרְאֵי שְׁמִי שֶׁמֶשׁ צְדָקָה

The Lord is speaking as if righteousness were the sun and that it would rise over the fearers of his name. He means that he will establish his righteous rule so that those who obey him are vindicated, honored, and blessed.
The Lord is using his name to represent all of him.
The Lord is speaking as if the sun had wings. He is using the image to speak of the arrival of the sun, which represents the effects of his establishing his reign.
The Lord is speaking as if the people would be so happy that they would go out and skip.
The point of this comparison is that just as calves that have been kept in a stall are very playful when they are let out, so the people will act very joyfully.
4:3: The Lord is speaking of the people’s victory over the wicked as if they would trample them.
The Lord is speaking of the complete defeat of the wicked as if they literally become ashes under the people’s feet.
4:4: The Lord is using the word Remember to mean obey by association with the way people need to remember something in order to obey it.
The Lord is speaking of two types of laws in order to include them and all other types of laws.
4:5: Malachi is using the phrase to the face to represent what is in front of someone or something. Here, the thing is a day that is described as though it were a person who is coming, so what is in front of the day is there before the day arrives. Therefore, to the face of the coming of means “before the coming of” the day.
